paragraphs: In washing the hands, the one washing must intend a washing that qualifies him for eating; therefore one does not wash the hands of a monkey, nor of a minor under six, since they have no thought or intention. Furthermore, even one who washed properly and intended the washing that qualifies him — he must still, through his thought and intention, guard the purity of his hands, so that if he let his mind wander from guarding his hands for a long while, then even though he does not know that his hands touched a soiled place, he must nevertheless go back and wash again. Thus one must keep his mind and intention fixed on the purity of his hands throughout the whole of his meal, this being because the essential expulsion of the sitra achra (the 'other side') was accomplished through his intention; therefore it is fitting that he not let his mind wander from this purity for as long as he is eating. To this the verse alludes (Ecclesiastes 9:7): "Go, eat your bread with simchah (joy), and drink your wine with a good heart, for God has already accepted your deeds" — for the letters of simchah (שמחה) are the letters of machshavah (thought), and it says that it is through the thought and through the good heart, which is the intention, that "God has accepted your deeds," for a deed alone, without the joining of intention and thought, does not rise to be accepted. And the name Elohim is used here in the manner I wrote above, for the seat of thought and intention is the brain and the heart, whose numerical value equals that of Elohim. Likewise the Torah, which is compared to eating and drinking, as it is written (Proverbs 9:5), "Come, eat of my bread, and drink of the wine I have mixed," is also harmed by a wandering mind, which is why the Almighty commanded (Deuteronomy 4:9): "Only take heed to yourself and guard your soul diligently, lest you forget the things your eyes have seen, and lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life" — and they said that "lest you forget" refers to the brain, where forgetfulness dwells, God forbid.

clarification.explanation: In washing the hands, the one washing must intend a washing that qualifies him for eating; therefore one does not wash the hands of someone who lacks the capacity to intend it (a monkey, or a minor under the age of six). And even if he washed properly and had the right intention, he must guard the purity of his hands in his thought throughout the entire meal — and if he let his mind wander from this for a long time, he must go back and wash again, even though he does not know for certain that his hands touched a soiled place, since the essential expulsion of impurity is accomplished through the intention; therefore it is forbidden to let one's mind wander from this purity for as long as one is eating. On this the Ben Ish Chai brings an allusion from the verse, "Go, eat your bread with joy... and drink your wine with a good heart, for God has already accepted your deeds": the word "besimchah" (with joy) has the same letters as "machshavah" (thought), and "a good heart" is the intention — and it is only through the joining of thought (in the brain) and intention (in the heart) that "God has accepted your deeds," for a deed alone, without intention and thought, does not rise to be accepted (and the name "Elohim" is alluded to here because the brain and heart, the seat of thought and intention, have the same numerical value as the name Elohim). The same applies to Torah study, which is compared to eating and drinking ("Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed") — there too, a wandering mind is harmful, which is why we were warned, "Only take heed to yourself and guard your soul diligently, lest you forget the things your eyes have seen... all the days of your life," for "lest you forget" corresponds to the brain, the seat of forgetfulness.
takeaways: The washing requires the intention of the one washing (not that of a monkey or minor), and one must maintain the intention for purity throughout the entire meal, not only at the moment of washing.

The verse "with joy... and with a good heart" alludes together to thought (in the brain) and intention (in the heart) — "besimchah" has the letters of "machshavah"; and likewise in Torah study a wandering mind is harmful, and "lest you forget" corresponds to the brain.

paragraphs: Just as a wandering mind interrupts eating and drinking with regard to the blessing, so too a change of place interrupts with regard to the blessing. And since opinions on this have multiplied, and we hold that in a doubt concerning blessings we are lenient, even against Maran of blessed memory whose rulings we have accepted, we shall therefore state the halachic ruling that the later authorities derived in order to fulfill one's obligation under the rule that a doubt concerning blessings is resolved leniently. It is this: if one dined somewhere, recited Hamotzi, and ate bread, and in the midst of his meal he changed his place — even going to another house, and even if he left no one at all at the table — if he let his mind wander from eating, then he must recite a blessing over items that are not part of the main meal, if he wishes to eat them, whether he eats them in the second house or in his original place after he returns to it afterward. But over items that are part of the main meal, he need not recite a blessing again, whether in the second house or when he returns to his original place, even though he let his mind wander — because as long as he is still within his meal, it is not considered the completion of the meal, since the bread requires that Birkat Hamazon be recited over it in its place. Therefore, when he gets up from his place to go elsewhere, his getting up is not the completion of his meal, even though he let his mind wander from eating, since he must still return to his place to recite Birkat Hamazon. Hence, when he returns and eats items that are part of the meal, with the intent of his original meal, he does so in order to complete his meal, and therefore he need not recite a blessing over them at the outset — all the more so when he returns and eats in his original place, which is the place of his meal, where he need not recite an opening blessing.

All this deals with a case where he already acted and changed his place; but at the outset, one must take care not to uproot himself from his meal and finish it elsewhere before reciting Birkat Hamazon, even if he left some of his companions at the table — because anything that requires an after-blessing in its place, due to its importance, one must bless it before departing from that place. For just as its importance is effective to prevent blessing it elsewhere, so too its importance is effective for this matter, that one must bless it before he departs — and even though he also eats in the second place and blesses there, so that he ends up reciting Birkat Hamazon in a place of eating, nevertheless, what does that help the first eating, which required a blessing in its place at the outset, before he departed on account of its importance? Except that if he has already departed, he need not go back and recite an opening blessing over what he eats in the second place, since that would not repair the wrong done by his departure; rather, since he must bless in a place of eating, he eats a little in the second place in order to then recite Birkat Hamazon there. Therefore, at the outset, one should not depart without a blessing; and even though, if he left some companions, this is not considered a departure if he intended to return to them — nevertheless, when he goes to finish his meal in another house, this is indeed a departure from his group.

This applies only where he did not intend at the outset, when he recited Hamotzi, to finish in another place — for then the fixing of his meal from the start was in this place, and therefore he must recite Birkat Hamazon in this place and not elsewhere. But if from the outset, when he recited Hamotzi, he intended to finish in another house, it is permitted to recite the blessing elsewhere, since from the start he did not fix his entire meal in this place — just as travelers are accustomed to eat along their way and then sit and bless in the place where they finish eating, since that was their intention from the start: not to fix a place for their eating in the place where they recited Hamotzi and began to eat.

In what case does this apply? When he departs from his first place and finishes his meal in the second place. But if he goes to the second place intending to return to his first place to finish his meal there, this is not considered a departure, even if he left no companions at all. Nevertheless, the Sages forbade doing so, because we are concerned lest he forget to return to his place to bless. And they permitted this only where he goes to another house and eats there, since, given that he eats there, he certainly will not forget the blessing, and it is not common for one to get up and go on his way without any blessing at all; therefore we say with certainty that when he gets up after eating in the second house, he will return to his first place to bless. Nevertheless, it is good that even in such a case he take care from the outset to leave one person at the table in the first place when he goes from there to the second place, and even if he does not happen to have anyone eating with him there, he should leave another person, even though that person did not eat with him there.

And all this is when he goes for a permissible matter, or even for a mitzvah, but one that is not time-bound (a mitzvah that is not fleeting); but for the sake of a time-bound mitzvah that cannot be postponed, such as the mitzvah of accompanying the dead or the like, or going to the synagogue to pray with the congregation — even though we say that if in the place he is going to he will not be eating, the Sages forbade doing so lest he forget to bless entirely — nevertheless, since it is for the sake of a time-bound mitzvah, it is permitted for him at the outset to go elsewhere to perform the mitzvah and to recite Birkat Hamazon when he returns to his place, and he need not even leave some companions at the table, since one should not delay a time-bound mitzvah out of concern that he might forget; see the Shulchan Aruch of the Gaon Rabbeinu Zalman of blessed memory and the other later authorities.

clarification.explanation: Just as a wandering mind during eating can require reciting the blessing again, so too a change of place may require reciting the blessing again; and since there is much dispute about this, the halachah (a doubt concerning blessings is resolved leniently) rules: one who dined in one place and recited Hamotzi, and in the midst of his meal moved to another place (even to another house, even without leaving anyone at the table) — if he let his mind wander from eating, he must recite a blessing over items that are not part of the main meal (such as fruit), if he wishes to eat them, whether in the new place or when he returns to the first place; but over items that are part of the main meal (meat, bread, and the like) he need not bless again, since his going was not considered "completion of the meal" (he still must return to his place to recite Birkat Hamazon). At the outset, one should not depart from the meal and finish it elsewhere before reciting Birkat Hamazon, unless from the very start, when he recited Hamotzi, he already intended to finish elsewhere (as is the way of travelers). And one who goes to another place intending to return — this is not a departure; nevertheless the Sages forbade doing so lest he forget to return and bless, and they permitted it only when he eats in the second place, and even then it is good to leave one person at the table, even someone who did not eat with him. An exception: when the going is for the sake of a time-bound mitzvah that cannot be postponed, such as accompanying the dead (the mitzvah of levayah) or praying with the congregation in the synagogue — it is permitted at the outset to go to the second place for the sake of fulfilling the mitzvah and to recite Birkat Hamazon only when he returns to his place, even without leaving anyone at the table; since one should not delay a time-bound mitzvah out of concern that he might forget to bless.
takeaways: Changing place in the middle of a meal: for the items of the meal itself (bread and its accompaniments) there is no new blessing; for additions (such as fruit) there is, if his mind wandered.

At the outset one should not depart from the place of the meal before Birkat Hamazon, unless this was his intention from the start (like travelers); and one who leaves intending to return should not do so unless he eats in the second place, and it is good to leave one person at the table.

For the sake of a time-bound mitzvah that cannot be postponed (such as accompanying the dead, or praying with the congregation) — it is permitted at the outset to leave the meal without leaving anyone at the table, and to recite Birkat Hamazon only upon returning.

paragraphs: Foods whose after-blessing is Me'ein Shalosh (the threefold blessing), as well as fruits of the seven species, and likewise wine, whose blessing is also Me'ein Shalosh — their law is like that of bread with regard to departing from one's place, in that it is forbidden to depart from one's place until one recites the after-blessing, since some say that just as bread requires its blessing in its place, so too these require their after-blessing in their place. Therefore, with regard to a change of place, we go leniently by the rule of a doubt concerning blessings, and we say their law is as we said above regarding bread: that if he got up from his first place and went to another courtyard, his standing up is not considered the completion of his meal, even though he let his mind wander from eating, since he must return to his place to recite the after-blessing. Therefore, when he returns and eats and drinks — even in another place — with the intent of his original meal, he does so to complete his meal; and all the more so if he returns to his original place and eats, that he need not recite an opening blessing, even if he left no companions at all.

clarification.explanation: Foods whose after-blessing is "Me'ein Shalosh" (cake and the like), and likewise fruits of the seven species, and likewise wine — their law regarding change of place is like that of bread: if he got up from his place and went to another courtyard, this is not considered the completion of his meal (he must return and recite the after-blessing in the original place), and therefore when he returns and eats or drinks them — even in another place — he does not bless again, and certainly not if he returns to his first place.
takeaways: Foods with the Me'ein Shalosh after-blessing, fruits of the seven species, and wine — their law regarding a change of place is like that of bread; they do not require a new blessing.

paragraphs: Foods and drinks whose after-blessing is Borei Nefashot Rabbot — these, according to everyone, do not require their after-blessing to be recited in the place of eating or drinking; rather, one is permitted to get up from his place before the after-blessing and recite the after-blessing elsewhere. Therefore, his getting up from his place to go elsewhere is the completion of his meal, and when he returns and eats in the second place he must recite an opening blessing, even though he has not yet recited the after-blessing over the eating in the first place. And even if he had intended in the first place to go to the second place and eat there, nevertheless, since he changed his place from this house to another house, he must bless what he eats in the second house; and likewise, if after going to the second house he returns to his first place and eats, he must bless what he eats. All this is when the change of place was from house to house; but if it was from room to room within a single house — if he had intended from the outset to eat in the second room, he need not go back and bless; but if he had not intended from the outset to eat in the second room, but afterward reconsidered and went to the second room and ate, he must go back and bless.

And even if he had not intended from the outset to eat in the second room, if he can see the first place, he does not go back and bless; and all the more so within a single room, from corner to corner, he does not go back and bless even if he had not intended this from the outset — since here there are two mitigating factors: that it is a single room, and also that he sees his first place. There are, however, those who disagree, and hold that a change is considered such even from corner to corner if he did not intend it, and all the more so if he cannot see the first place; therefore, at the outset one should take care not to change at all. And one must warn the multitude of people about this, for this matter is common and frequent among people, who get up in the middle of a meal from their fixed table in one room and enter another room for some purpose, and find fruit there and eat without a blessing, thinking they are exempt since they already blessed over the fruit on the table — but in truth this is a change from room to room, and even if they had intended this from the outset, as long as they cannot see their first place they must bless, and all the more so where they had not intended this from the outset.

clarification.explanation: Foods and drinks whose after-blessing is "Borei Nefashot Rabbot" — according to everyone, their after-blessing need not be recited in the place of eating, and one may get up and bless elsewhere. Therefore, his getting up from his place is considered the completion of his meal with regard to them: when he returns and eats in a new place, he must recite an opening blessing — even if he intended in advance to move there, and even if he later returns to his first place. This is when the move was from house to house; but from room to room within the same house — if he had intended from the outset to eat in the second room, he need not bless again; and if he reconsidered without prior intention, he must bless. And even without prior intention, if he can see his first place from the second room, he does not go back and bless (and all the more so from corner to corner within the same room).
takeaways: Foods whose after-blessing is "Borei Nefashot Rabbot" — moving from house to house requires a new opening blessing.
Moving from room to room: if he intended this in advance, or he can see his first place, he does not bless again.

paragraphs: Although we wrote above that anything whose after-blessing is Me'ein Shalosh has the law of bread, both with regard to blessing in the place where one fixed his eating and with regard to a change of place, as mentioned above — this is specifically when he eats a kezayit (an olive's volume), so that he becomes obligated in the after-blessing. But if he did not eat a kezayit, its law is like that of items whose after-blessing is "Borei Nefashot Rabbot," which do not require the after-blessing in their place. And even when eating a kezayit of them, if from the outset he did not intend to fix a place for his eating, but rather held them in his hand and ate while walking — as is the way of people who sometimes take pastry or other fruits in their hand and eat them while walking through the house from room to room — there is no law of change of place in this, and he recites the after-blessing in the place where he finishes eating. For even with bread, travelers are accustomed to eat along their way and bless in the place where they finish eating, and there is no concern in this, as I wrote above.

clarification.explanation: The previous ruling (that foods with the Me'ein Shalosh after-blessing have the law of bread regarding change of place) applies only when one ate a kezayit and has already become obligated in the after-blessing; but if he did not eat a kezayit, their law is like that of items whose after-blessing is "Borei Nefashot Rabbot" (not requiring a blessing in their place). Likewise, even if he ate a kezayit, if from the outset he did not fix a place for his eating but held the fruit in his hand and ate while walking from room to room (as people are accustomed to take fruit and eat it while walking) — this is not considered a change of place, and he recites the after-blessing in the place where he finishes eating.
takeaways: Eating less than a kezayit, or eating while walking without fixing a place — these do not carry the law of change of place.

paragraphs: One who ate bread or other items whose blessing is Me'ein Shalosh, who — as we said — is not permitted at the outset to go finish his meal elsewhere before reciting the after-blessing: if he transgressed the ruling of the Sages and left his place without blessing, whether he left deliberately or inadvertently, he should return to his place and bless, provided the place is not so far that there is concern the food will be digested in his stomach by the time he returns. And although the later authorities wrote a remedy for this, that he eat a kezayit of bread in the second place and bless there, this remedy is not clear to my mind, since it introduces a doubt concerning the blessing of Hamotzi. There is, however, another remedy agreed upon by all: that another person eat a kezayit of bread and recite Hamotzi over it, intending to exempt this person; and if this is not possible for him, he must return to his place and bless.

In what case does this apply? Where it is possible for him to return; but if he is traveling on the road and no one is waiting for him, then even if he left deliberately, he need not return to his place, since after the fact, if he blessed in the place mentioned, we hold that he has fulfilled his obligation in any case, and a case of pressing need is treated like a case after the fact. Likewise, if the first place where he ate is unclean and he cannot clean it now, he may go outside and bless, even though he does not eat in the second place; and in this case too, where he leaves this place for the second place on account of cleanliness, if he happens to find in the second place someone who will eat and bless with the intent to include him, how good and how pleasant; see Chesed LaAlafim, siman 184, se'if katan 1.

clarification.explanation: One who ate bread or an item whose blessing is Me'ein Shalosh, and transgressed the ruling and left his place before reciting the after-blessing (deliberately or inadvertently) — should return to his place and bless, provided the place is not too far (lest the food be digested). One should not rely on the remedy of eating a kezayit of bread in the new place and blessing there (since that itself introduces a doubt concerning the blessing of Hamotzi); rather, the agreed-upon remedy is that another person eat a kezayit of bread and recite Hamotzi with the intent to exempt him. If this is not possible, he must return to his place. But if he is on the road and cannot return, or if the first place is unclean, he may bless in the place where he finds himself (a case of pressing need is treated like after the fact).
takeaways: Left his place without reciting the after-blessing — he returns to bless, or has another person recite Hamotzi and exempt him.
Unable to return (on the road, or an unclean place) — he blesses in the place where he finds himself.

paragraphs: Even for a minor reason, one is permitted to get up and move from here to there within a single place, within four amot, and bless there, since four amot are considered a single place with regard to many matters; but beyond four amot, one should not bless on account of a minor reason, but only for a major reason and a strong necessity that compels him to do so; see Chayei Adam, klal 47, letter vav. And one who is careful even within four amot, a blessing shall come upon him.

clarification.explanation: Even for a minor reason, one is permitted to get up and move within four amot in the same place and bless there, since four amot are considered a single place for many purposes; but beyond four amot, one should not bless from there on account of a minor reason, but only for a major reason and a genuine necessity.
takeaways: A change of place within four amot is not considered a change of place at all — one may bless there for any reason.

paragraphs: One who needs to relieve himself in the middle of his meal — this is not considered an interruption, and he need not bless again when he returns and eats; and even the blessing over washing the hands he need not recite again, since there is a dispute about this and a doubt concerning blessings is resolved leniently — he should merely contemplate the blessing of Al Netilat Yadayim in his heart.

clarification.explanation: One who goes out to relieve himself (to the bathroom) in the middle of his meal — this is not considered an interruption, and he need not bless again when he returns and eats. And he need not recite the blessing on washing the hands again either (due to the dispute — a doubt concerning blessings is resolved leniently), but should merely contemplate the blessing in his heart.
takeaways: Leaving to relieve oneself in the middle of a meal is not an interruption; and one need not bless again on washing the hands (only contemplate it).

paragraphs: If he interrupted his meal in order to pray, then even though this is not considered an interruption with regard to the blessing, nevertheless he should wash his hands without reciting the blessing on washing the hands, since there is a dispute about this; and if he has no water, he may rely on those who are lenient.

clarification.explanation: One who interrupted his meal in order to pray — even though this is not considered an interruption with regard to Birkat Hamazon — should nonetheless wash his hands without a blessing (due to the dispute); and if he has no water, he may rely on those who are lenient.
takeaways: Interrupting the meal to pray — one washes the hands without a blessing upon returning.

paragraphs: If one ate fruit in one garden and went to another garden, he must go back and bless again, even if the gardens are adjacent, and even if when he first blessed he had already intended this. The same law applies within a single garden: if he had not intended from the outset to eat from all the trees, he must bless again over each and every tree he reconsiders and decides to eat from — and even if he ate on the eastern side of a fig tree and comes to eat on its western side, he must go back and bless if he had not intended this from the outset. And this is not specific to garden fruit alone, but applies to anywhere one eats items that do not require a new blessing in their place — the law is the same.

In what case does this apply? When the garden is enclosed by partitions; but if it is not enclosed by partitions, his intention does not extend to all the trees, but rather the matter depends on whether he can see his first place: if from the second place he sees his first place, he does not bless again; and if he does not see it, whether on account of distance or on account of some partition between them, he blesses again. And in my holy book Mikabtzi'el I investigated, with God's help: if he does not see all of his place but only part of it, what is the law? And if you should say that seeing part of it suffices, and one need not see all of it — then what if he sees it while standing, but does not see it while sitting? Now, where he stands and eats, we have no question; but the question arises when he sits and eats and does not see it — do we say that since he would see it if he stood, this is effective, or perhaps it is not effective? And if you should say that since he would see it if he stood, this is effective — then what if he was standing inside a pit and does not see it from there, as opposed to standing at the edge of the pit, from where he does see it? And there I brought, with God's help, what I wrote in the Gemara, Zevachim 118, that all these doubts arise regarding the eating of sacred things in view of Shiloh, and the first doubt is resolved from there, that seeing part suffices, for so it was obvious to Rav Pappa there; and what is written in the baraita, "It was taught: one who sees, they meant one who sees the whole of it, etc." — this is not the correct text, as "Tzon Kodashim" wrote, and the other doubts in our case are the very questions of Rav Pappa and Rabbi Yirmeyah there, which remained unresolved (teiku); see what "Chok Natan" of blessed memory wrote regarding the intent of "if you should say," which is said there — and it is known that there is a dispute as to whether "if you should say" is itself a settled ruling or not. Therefore, since the Talmud there concludes with teiku, so too the doubts in our case remain in doubt, and one should not bless; what should he do? He should bring another person to bless with the intent to exempt him, and then eat. And there, in my holy book Mikabtzi'el, I wrote that all these doubts are relevant to the law of the Megillah, in siman 698, regarding walled cities whose neighboring villages are seen with them and read the Megillah on the same day as they do; see there. And there I raised what may be asked from the Gemara in Megillah, page 3b, regarding the distinction that Rabbi Yirmeyah makes, such as "if you sat in a valley," etc., and regarding the very question that Rabbi Yirmeyah himself raises in the aforementioned Gemara in Zevachim. And I then made a proper distinction between the case in Megillah and the aforementioned case in Zevachim, and I concluded, in any event, that our case here, regarding blessings over fruit, is indeed comparable to that case in Zevachim.

clarification.explanation:
One who ate fruit in one garden and moved to another garden must bless again, even if the gardens are adjacent and even if when he first blessed he had already intended to eat in the second garden as well. And the same applies within the very same garden: if he had not intended from the outset to eat from all the trees, he must bless anew on each tree he reconsiders and decides to eat from — and even if he ate on the eastern side of a fig tree and comes to eat on its western side, he must go back and bless if he had not intended this in advance. This law is not specific to garden fruit, but applies to any place where one eats items that do not require a new blessing, as long as one remains within that same "place."
When does this ruling (that an intention from the start of the meal exempts the whole garden) apply? When the garden is enclosed by partitions. But if the garden is not enclosed by partitions, the initial intention does not suffice for all the trees; rather, everything depends on whether, from the new place, he can still see his first place: if he can see it, he does not bless again; if he cannot see it (whether on account of distance or on account of some partition between them), he blesses anew.
The Ben Ish Chai adds that in his book Mikabtzi'el he raised several practical doubts on this matter: What is the law if he sees only part of his first place and not all of it — is this sufficient? And what is the law if he sees his place while standing, but does not see it while sitting? And what is the law if he was standing inside a pit and cannot see from there, as opposed to standing at the edge of the pit, from where he can see it? He discusses these questions by comparing them to similar doubts raised by the Sages in the Talmud (in Zevachim, and in the laws of the Megillah regarding walled cities), some of which remained there unresolved ("teiku"). His practical conclusion: since these doubts remain without a clear resolution, one should not bless out of doubt. The practical solution is to bring another person who will bless with the intent to exempt him, and only then to eat.
takeaways: Ate in one garden and moved to an adjacent garden — a new blessing is required, even if he intended in advance to eat in both.
In a garden enclosed by partitions, an intention from the start of eating exempts all the trees in it; in a garden not enclosed by partitions, it depends on whether he can see his previous place.

When there is doubt as to whether he can see his previous place (for example, he sees it standing but not sitting, or he stood inside a pit and did not see from there) — it is best not to bless himself, but to bring another person who will bless and exempt him. (Seeing only part of his previous place is considered sufficient and does not require a new blessing.)

paragraphs: If he finished his meal and washed his hands with Mayim Acharonim (the final water), and likewise if he said "Hav lan u'nevareich" ("give us [water], and let us bless"), even though he has not yet washed his hands — he can no longer eat or drink until he recites Birkat Hamazon. And although there is a dispute about all this, with several differing opinions, this is nonetheless the essential ruling in practice, due to the doubt concerning blessings. For if he did not wash his hands and did not say "Hav lan u'nevareich," but merely decided in his heart not to eat anymore, or cleared the table, or said "give us [water] and let us wash our hands" without saying "and let us bless" — then, according to everyone, he is permitted to bring items that require a blessing before them, such as fruit or drinks that he had not yet blessed during the meal, and to bless over them; but items over which he already blessed during the meal, he should not eat, on account of the doubt concerning the blessing, since there is a dispute about this, and he should not knowingly enter into a doubt concerning blessings. All this is when he decided in his mind not to eat anymore; but if he said "Hav lan u'nevareich" while intending to continue eating until they bring him water to wash his hands, then he is permitted to eat according to everyone, and he need not bless again; see Chesed LaAlafim. And one who relies on the table of others (a guest) — even if he said "Hav lan u'nevareich," this is not considered a wandering of the mind, if the host does not wish it, since presumably his mind is dependent on the will of the host. However, if at the time he said this he clearly let his mind wander, deciding firmly that even if the host does not wish it and asks him to eat and drink more, he will make his excuses and not eat or drink — this is considered a wandering of the mind. And if the host said "Hav lan u'nevareich" and they all remained silent and agreed to his words, this is considered a wandering of the mind for all of them; but if one of them did not agree to his words and intended to eat more, it is not considered a wandering of the mind for this person, and he may eat and drink.

clarification.explanation:
One who finished his meal and washed with Mayim Acharonim, and likewise one who said "Hav lan u'nevareich" (even though he has not yet washed) — can no longer eat or drink until he recites Birkat Hamazon. And although there are several differing opinions about all this, this is the essential ruling in practice, on account of the doubt concerning blessings.
But if he did not wash and did not say "Hav lan u'nevareich," but merely decided in his heart not to eat anymore, or cleared the table, or said "give us [water] and let us wash" without "and let us bless" — then according to everyone he is permitted to eat items that require a blessing before them (such as fruit or drinks he had not yet blessed during the meal), and to bless over them; but items he already blessed during the meal, he should not eat, on account of the doubt, so as not to knowingly enter into a doubt concerning blessings.
All this is when he decided in his mind not to eat anymore; but if he said "Hav lan u'nevareich" while intending to continue eating until they bring him water to wash — he is permitted to eat according to everyone, and need not bless again.
And one who relies on another's table (a guest) — even if he said "Hav lan u'nevareich," this is not a wandering of the mind, since his mind is dependent on the will of the host — unless he clearly decided in his heart not to eat anymore, even if the host asks him to. And if the host said "Hav lan u'nevareich" and everyone remained silent and agreed — this is a wandering of the mind for all of them; but one who did not agree and intended to eat more, it is not a wandering of the mind for him, and he may eat and drink.
takeaways: Mayim Acharonim, or "Hav lan u'nevareich" — one may not eat or drink until Birkat Hamazon (on account of the doubt concerning blessings).
Deciding in his heart alone, or merely clearing the table — permits eating new items with a blessing, but not items already blessed.
A guest — "Hav lan u'nevareich" is not a wandering of the mind unless he firmly decided so; silent agreement by all present is a wandering of the mind for all of them.

paragraphs: If it is the local custom, when there is a group eating and drinking and someone comes in from outside and joins them, that each one hands him a cup — he should bless only over the first cup, since presumably when he blessed, his mind was on everything they would give him afterward. Nevertheless, it is good to intend explicitly at the outset, when he blesses, to exempt all the cups that will be given to him afterward.

clarification.explanation: If it is the local custom that when a person joins a group that is drinking from outside, they hand him cups one after another — he blesses only over the first cup, since his mind was generally on everything they would give him; nevertheless, it is good to intend explicitly in advance, in his first blessing, to exempt all the cups to come.
takeaways: One who joins a group drinking cups blesses only over the first one (an explicit prior intention is preferable).
